newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Peace beckons after pardon for Khmer Rouge leader.
newsitem.headline: Peace beckons after pardon for Khmer Rouge leader.

text.p: A royal pardon for dissident Khmer Rouge leader Ieng Sary should put Cambodian peace talks back on track but many find it hard to stomach amnesty for the former foreign minister of the guerrillas' murderous 1975-79 regime.
Ieng Sary had been sentenced to death in absentia for his role in the deaths of more than a million people from execution, disease, starvation or overwork in labour camps.

"I consider (the amnesty) a golden opportunity for the Cambodian people to end the war and for national reconciliation," co-Premier Hun Sen told Reuters on Saturday, adding that military commanders of both sides would resume talks in the next few days.
But a western diplomat, asking for anonymity, hinted that the amnesty could present some foreign policy complications.

"We think its going to cause some consternation in the international community," he said. Others said some western nations would review aid to reflect disquiet that a notorious criminal was being forgiven for his part in abuses.

King Norodom Sihanouk signed the amnesty on Saturday in the interests of reconciliation and at the request of co-Premiers Prince Norodom Ranariddh and Hun Sen, but he also clearly had reservations about pardoning a man he has long disliked.

Sihanouk wrote to Amnesty International chief Pierre Sane on Friday saying he would always support as an ordinary citizen the convening of any future international trial of the leaders of the late 1970s killing fields rule, including top leader Pol Pot and Ieng Sary.

Ieng Sary, foreign minister and deputy premier in Pol Pot's 1975-79 regime, said on September 8 that he was not involved in the genocide during the Khmer Rouge reign and added that the government should clear up his legal status before peace talks could advance.
The Khmer Rouge, then in alliance with Ranariddh and Sihanouk, fought Hun Sen's Vietnamese-backed government until signing a United Nations brokered peace accord in 1993.
They reneged on that pact and have been fighting the coalition between Ranariddh and Hun Sen that emerged out of general elections in 1993.
Ieng Sary and thousands of guerrillas along Cambodia's northwest border with Thailand split from the mainstream Khmer Rouge last month and struck a ceasefire with the government.
A human rights worker, who asked not to be named, said he had spoken to many people who found government dealings with Ieng Sary abhorrent, but equal numbers who were more pragmatic.
"Two sentiments exist. One, 'what the hell let's give the amnesty and get on with it' and the other 'we can't give amnesty to mass murderers.'"

Analysts said the government appeared keen to wrap up reconciliation talks with the breakaway Khmer Rouge guerrillas quickly, noting that Hun Sen had pushed Ranariddh to urge the king to grant an amnesty as soon as possible.
"The whole process of negotiations with the Ieng Sary faction has been in a hurry," said an Asian analyst.
He said the premiers seemed determined to "rush headlong so that nobody would be able to stop it (peace) because the momentum is so much."

Hun Sen said the king had agreed to the pardon after two-thirds of the 120-member parliament had signed the motion, but MPs contacted on Sunday said they had not been consulted and were surprised there had been no debate.

Kem Sokha, an MP of the Buddhist Liberal Democratic Party, said he believed the voice of the people should have been heard through their elected representatives and added that parliament could not be held responsible if anything went wrong.

But the analyst said if Sihanouk had signed without a formal debate, "he must have got some pretty good assurances from the two PMs that the negotiations are genuine and that eight (Khmer Rouge) divisions, not just four, are defecting and that the rift looks real."

In the meantime, the government is expected to reopen talks with the dissident guerrillas on how to join forces and administer areas held by Ieng Sary loyalists, while at the same time encouraging further defections from the hardline group.
